## The idea

A note can feel like one object even when its waveform contains several frequencies. That apparent contradiction is the beginning of timbre. Start with a sine wave at 220 Hz, then add sine waves at 440, 660, and 880 Hz. Because all four begin together and share a whole-number relationship, the ear tends to gather them into one pitched sound rather than a four-note melody.

Each component is a *partial*. When partial frequencies occur at `1f`, `2f`, `3f`, `4f`, and so on, they belong to the *harmonic series* above a fundamental frequency `f`. Their relative amplitudes help determine the sound's colour. The program represents that colour as a short profile of `[multiple, level]` pairs and builds it one component at a time.

Listen first to the bare 220 Hz sine. Keep that thin reference in mind as the upper components enter. Pitch should remain anchored near A3 while brightness and edge accumulate around it.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 60

base_hz = 220.0
partials = [[1, 0.8], [2, 0.35], [3, 0.2], [4, 0.12]]

define :additive_tone do |base, profile|
  profile.each do |multiple, level|
    synth :sine, note: hz_to_midi(base * multiple), amp: level,
      attack: 0.05, sustain: 1.5, release: 0.4
  end
  sleep 2.2
end

1.upto(partials.length) do |count|
  additive_tone base_hz, partials.take(count)
  sleep 0.5
end
```

The first pass contains only the fundamental and should sound plain, with little internal colour. Each following pass retains everything heard before and adds one higher partial. You may hear a brighter or firmer edge rather than a separate new pitch. The last pass is also louder in total, so keep the level moderate and distinguish increased energy from the particular colour added by the upper frequencies.

## Change one thing

1. Make every amplitude `0.25`. The fundamental loses its dominance and the upper partials become unusually prominent. Listen for a harder, thinner compound tone as well as the change in total loudness.

2. Restore the profile, then remove the second partial while retaining the third and fourth. The fundamental still identifies the pitch, but the missing octave component leaves a different balance above it. Describe the gap by comparing the altered profile directly with the original.

3. Restore the full profile and change the base from 220 to 165 Hz. Every component moves because it is derived from the same base. The harmonic relationships survive in a lower register, although the speaker and your hearing may make the balance seem different.

These comparisons isolate amplitude profile, missing components, and fundamental frequency. Restore the reference between them so one audible cause remains in view.

## Why it works

Additive synthesis builds a complex waveform by summing simpler ones. In this profile, frequency multipliers choose the components and amplitude values act as their weights. The fundamental supplies the main repetition rate and a strong pitch cue. The upper components reshape the waveform within each cycle, which changes timbre without requiring a new fundamental.

The components fuse partly because their cycles repeatedly align. At 220 Hz, the fundamental completes one cycle while 440 completes two, 660 completes three, and 880 completes four. After the fundamental's cycle, all four return to a shared boundary. That repeating compound pattern supports the impression of one note.

This four-sine sound is a model, not a complete account of an acoustic instrument. Real tones often begin with noise, change spectral balance during the note, and contain components that do not sit at exact integer multiples. The small model is useful because it exposes one mechanism without hiding it inside a preset synth.

Amplitude needs care whenever signals are added. Four components at `0.8` can produce a much larger combined peak than any one synth call suggests. The falling levels in the original profile provide headroom and resemble the declining upper spectrum of many sounds. If an edited profile distorts, lower all its levels before drawing a conclusion about timbre. Distortion introduces its own upper frequencies and can make loudness masquerade as brightness.

The profile also shows why musical data is often more informative before playback. You can inspect the multiples, compare two amplitude curves, or calculate the highest frequency without rendering a note. Sound then gives those numbers perceptual meaning. Lesson 5 builds on the same alignment idea: when two fundamentals have a small whole-number ratio, some of the partials above them coincide.

## Take it further

Build two four-partial profiles above the same 220 Hz fundamental. Give the first a steep amplitude decline. In the second, strengthen the third and fourth partials while keeping enough headroom to avoid distortion. Alternate the profiles four times without changing their base frequency or envelope.

Print both profiles and identify the partial whose amplitude differs most. Then audition the alternation in Sonic Pi 5 at a moderate level. Describe the change using a feature you can point to, such as a harder edge, a more hollow middle, or stronger brightness. The unchanged pitch is part of the result: the exercise succeeds when the colour changes while A3 remains the centre you hear.
